name: Cognitive Rehabilitation
title: Cognitive Rehabilitation
answer: Cognitive rehabilitation uses structured exercises and compensatory strategies to improve attention, memory, executive function, language, and social cognition after acquired brain injury, stroke, or in progressive conditions. AI in this area includes adaptive training software, speech and language analysis, and models that estimate a person's current cognitive capacity from task performance or interaction patterns. The scope covers both restorative approaches, which aim to rebuild underlying skills, and compensatory approaches, which teach workarounds and environmental supports. It also includes remote monitoring and delivery through apps and telehealth platforms.

AI in this area includes adaptive training software, speech and language analysis, and models that estimate a person's current cognitive capacity from task performance or interaction patterns. The scope covers both restorative approaches, which aim to rebuild underlying skills, and compensatory approaches, which teach workarounds and environmental supports. It also includes remote monitoring and delivery through apps and telehealth platforms.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on consumer devices such as tablets, smartphones, and laptops, with some clinical setups using dedicated workstations or virtual reality headsets. Cloud services handle model inference, data storage, and progress dashboards for clinicians, while on-device processing is used where latency or privacy matters. The underlying models are often smaller than large language models, relying on classifiers, reinforcement learning for adaptive difficulty, and speech or handwriting recognition. Integration with electronic health records is common but uneven.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by collecting repeated performance data from exercises, such as reaction times, accuracy, error types, and voice features, then fitting models that adjust task difficulty and select next steps. Clinicians set goals and review dashboards, while the software provides cues, spaced repetition, and feedback. Some systems use natural language processing to score narrative recall or conversational turn-taking. The models are usually supervised or reinforcement learning based, trained on labeled patient sessions or normative data.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on data protection, because cognitive performance data can reveal sensitive health information and may be used to make eligibility or capacity judgments. Consent, data minimization, and clear retention rules are important, as is the risk that an algorithm misjudges a patient's progress or fails to flag deterioration. Liability questions arise when an automated recommendation replaces or delays clinician review. Provenance of training data matters, since models built on narrow populations may not transfer across ages, languages, or injury types.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more personalized, home based programs that combine passive sensing from phones or wearables with active exercises, giving clinicians a continuous picture of cognitive change. Multimodal models may link speech, gaze, and motor signals to detect subtle improvements or declines earlier. There is also work on using generative models to create realistic social scenarios for practicing communication and executive skills. The field is moving toward hybrid care, where AI handles routine adaptation and human therapists handle goal setting and complex judgment.
